title: Coins - the first form of money
articleHtml:
A 

Few people pay much attention to coins. There is even a belief that they will one day be obsolete and money will at last have achieved the pure status of a mathematical formulation.


B 

Coins are among the most durable of our artefacts, and future archaeologists will scrutinise coins in order to learn about their distant ancestors. There are thousands of different coins each designed to carry meaning as well as value.


C 

Before coins, trade was based on barter: the direct trade of commodities. Metal coins were far more portable. The Greeks, however, were the first to realise the full potential of the new invention. They were a trading people of seafarers. Their civilsation, which was composed of dozens of city-states, was highly decentralised.

 

D 

The value of coins was generally based on the intrinsic value of the metal they were made of. At first this was mostly silver. Had the Greek silver mining been on larger scale,it could have caused problems similar to those faced by the Spanish centuries later, when so much gold from the New World was brought into their economy that it resulted in serious inflation. One advantage of straightedge value was that coins could be weighed to determine the amount of metal they contained. Greeks realised that different metals have different-volume ratios and that by measuring the amount of displacement when coins were immersed in water.

 

E 

All ancient coins were made by hand using engraved metal moulds. The endless variety encountered in coins with the same designs is due to the fact that the moulds had to be remade repeatedly, by many different artisans. One of the distinctive features of coins, in fact, is that they are the work of anonymous craftsmen. Coins were a way of advertising the qualities of each particular city-state.

 

F 

Greek coins' uniform design is the beautiful features of the city's patron, Athena (with her owl on the reverse of the coin), which seem to have been repeated virtually unaltered for many years.

 

G 

One side of a coin was always occupied by the head of a divinity, so it was a relatively small step, at around 323 BC, for Greek coins to replace that head with the portrait of the reigning monarch, a tradition that has continued in monarchies to the present day.
